cells.tense: Right now you can hold several true readings of a situation and still know what to do.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Before anyone asks, tell the people it concerns what you've settled on and where it goes — plainly, no defending. Put it out and walk away from it.
cells.core:
You see more sides of a situation than most people standing in it, and it doesn't scatter you. More readings arrive and you can hold them and still know what to do next. What's steady in you is structure that actually serves what it holds up, so things make sense around you and people find their footing without being told to.

Something's waiting on your say-so this week, and you've been holding several good versions instead of putting one of them down. Before anyone asks, tell the people it concerns what you've settled on and where it goes — plainly, no defending. You may still turn out to be partly wrong, and that won't matter. What people need isn't the perfect reading. It's knowing what the shape is.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold many true readings and still name what comes first.
cells.verb: Holding many true readings at once without forcing them into one.
cells.place: Where something gets set down on purpose so the hands are free.

cells.tense: Where you see clearly, some version of this will have to be decided before you feel ready.
cells.act: face one way for three days
cells.ask: Pick one direction out of what you've been weighing and face it for three days without surveying the rest. You can go back after.
cells.core:
Your reading runs ahead of itself. Every angle gets held, and then every angle of the angle, because somewhere in all of it is the correct one and choosing early feels like losing. It's a kind of bracing — rehearsing decisions that haven't arrived yet, wearing a future nobody can write in yet.

You don't have to settle anything for good. Pick one direction out of everything you've been weighing and face it for three days without surveying the rest. Then you can go back. What's yours to offer isn't the widest view; it's a light you actually move toward. Three days of steering by one of them tells you what a week of comparing can't — not whether it's right, whether it holds you.
cells.sheetLine: Comparing is not the same as steering.

cells.tense: Where you see clearly, you are standing at a threshold the rest of you already crossed.
cells.act: join someone in the work so the two streams run as one
cells.ask: Take one person you work or live alongside and join their task this week — an hour at their pace, finished together, no leading.
cells.core:
Where your reading is meant to open into the next thing, some of you is still back at the last one. A passage you already walked through is the one you keep standing at, and it takes the place where new seeing would go. You're not confused. You're elsewhere. That's why new situations land blunted — you meet them from a room you've already left.

Rather than pushing at your own feeling, go in through company. Take one person you work alongside or live with, and join their task this week — an hour, at their pace, finished together, no leading. Two hands on one thing beats one more pass through your own head. Whatever gets made is small. What matters is that something you can see got made, now, with you in it.

cells.tense: You keep reading the people around you accurately and calling it nothing much.
cells.act: act on the private sense of what is right
cells.ask: Next time you feel what's fair in a situation, act on it in the moment instead of filing it — say the fair thing, make the fair move, and move on without marking it.
cells.core:
You read what's fair in a room quickly, and quietly, and then file it under nothing — the move you made, the thing you didn't say, the read that turned out exactly right. Nobody hands you credit and you don't take any. You've been blaming the timing, or the situation, or luck. The fairness was yours. It's still running even while you discount it at the door.

Start with the next case. When you feel what's fair, act on it then instead of filing it — say the fair thing, make the fair move, and move on without marking it. If you're wrong about your own part in how you see people, you've still done the fair thing, and no one is worse off. If you're right, you'll notice the account settling in the direction you already knew.
cells.sheetLine: You read what's fair and call it nothing much.
